title: 🔭 Mercury at Greatest Eastern Elongation — Evening Star
description:
Mercury reaches its greatest angular separation from the Sun (18.1°) — the best window to spot the innermost planet this apparition. Look west after sunset: Mercury appears as a bright, steady point low in the western sky after sunset.

At 18.1°, this is a shallow elongation — Mercury sits deep in the twilight glow and will be a challenge to spot. Binoculars are recommended; look precisely where the Sun set (or will rise). Mercury never rises far from the Sun; it always stays close to the horizon near sunrise or sunset and is only visible for a brief window each apparition.

title: 🔭 Venus at Greatest Eastern Elongation — Evening Star
description:
Venus reaches its greatest angular separation from the Sun (45.9°) — its best position as the Evening Star this apparition. Look for it blazing in the western sky after sunset, far outshining every star and planet. At 45.9° from the Sun, Venus enjoys a long viewing window of well over an hour in a dark sky before it follows the Sun below the horizon.

At this elongation Venus shows a roughly half-lit phase through a telescope — like a tiny half-moon, with a disk noticeably larger than any planet appears to the naked eye.
